Thank you for the opportunity to present to you today, and I hope that this presentation will be helpful in providing you with an update on work underway in NAFO to incorporate connectivity and climate change into scientific advice for management decisions on VMEs. It has been more than 2 decades since international policy for sustainable fisheries has called for the protection of vulnerable marine ecosystems. Systems from the harmful effects of bottom contact fishing, and in that time significant progress has been made on their identification, distribution, ecosystem role, and protection. Since the last bottom fishing workshop, 2 additional elements have been introduced into policy: connectivity and climate change. Connectivity was introduced in 2022, while the impacts of climate change which were first identified in 2016, were further elaborated on by 2022. Identifying areas where deepwater species and VMEs are likely to better survive climate impacts, and conversely areas where the fauna will experience new environments and so may be subject to additional physiological stresses, are critical elements for conservation planning. Both connectivity and climate change impacts can be assessed using high-resolution ocean model products, which are readily available for all of the world's oceans. Connectivity can be assessed by modeling particle dispersal to mimic transport of gametes and larvae using data on current velocities from the ocean models. Species distribution models predict species habitats by correlating known species locations with environmental factors, predict presence in unsampled areas. These models can use present-day and projected future climate data alongside chosen climate models and emission scenarios to map potential species ranges. The outcome is a prediction of habitat suitability showing areas where a species might persist, colonize, or decline, offering critical data for conservation and management decisions. For example, here the presence probability of the bubblegum coral along the Scotian Shelf is predicted using ocean model projections to mid-century. 2045 to 2065. Areas in red show areas of high probability of presence for this species. Identification of climate refugia, or areas where environmental conditions are predicted to remain unchanged in future, can help in identifying areas where VMEs are likely to better survive. Areas in green identify the climate refugia for the bubblegum coral at mid-century. While areas in yellow show where one of the variables in the model falls outside of the conditions previously experienced, and so will require adaptation—a property for which we have very little information on, but which can affect survivorship and reproduction. In NAFO, connectivity modeling and species distribution modeling have been undertaken. to assess and prioritize climate-induced impacts. A suite of ocean model products from 22 CMIP6 models, the latest generation of fully released global ocean and climate models, were ensembled and statistically downscaled using neural networking. Species distribution models were run using 44 water column variables projected for 4 time periods under each of 4 emission scenarios. In addition to the water column variables, one static variable associated with the terrain, or the sea floor, was also used to anchor the predictions. I won't have time to go into details of this modeling, but species distribution modeling is significantly more complex under future conditions. While present-day modeling requires correlating known species occurrences with current environmental data, Future projections introduce added layers of uncertainty, which need to be examined and interpreted. Next is a preview of our results for the black coral to illustrate how this information can be used to inform management decisions. Black corals are very long-lived, with some aged over 1,000 years, and individuals present today are likely to be present at the end of this The dominant species in the NAFO study area is called Stauropathys arctica, shown on the right. This is a large coral found from the tail of Grand Bank and Flemish Cap north to Greenland and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Species distribution modeling shows the climate refugia for the black coral in gray and areas of univariate extrapolation Causing novel environments in orange for the reference period and the 4 successive time periods to the end of century under SSP2 4.5, which is a middle-of-the-road emission scenario and one suggested for climate planning and risk assessments. You can see the progressive loss of climate refugia in gray over time. Climate refugia in P1 are shown in yellow in relation to the black coral VMEs shown by red polygons and the closed areas shown in blue outline. The largest VMEs are labeled in order of their size on the left panel. 3 of the 4 largest VMEs are in climate refugia in the near term, as shown by the green coloring. While one, BC-4, will experience a novel environment with unknown consequences. Overlaying the closures on the right panel shows that all but BC-4 have partial protection under the present-day closures, with BC-2 the best protected. Such overlays can be useful in discussing management options to improve conservation effectiveness. By mid-century, there are 2 large VME areas on Flemish Cap that are expected to be under novel environmental conditions, as they do not overlap with the yellow areas. Monitoring of those areas can help to inform whether the corals are showing adaptive responses. Identification of the variable causing the novel conditions can help to determine adaptation potential. The variables responsible for creating the novel environments under P1 and P2 are primarily the minimum bottom temperature and the mean mixed layer depth in summer. Depth is a static variable in that it doesn't change, and so although there are areas outside of the depth range for this species, it is not changing over time. Looking more closely at minimum bottom temperature, there is warming through to end of century with temperatures above 7.5 degrees Celsius for large areas. This information can be used to assess adaptation potential and to inform thermal stress experiments in the lab. Connectivity was separately assessed using the particle tracking models mentioned previously and used to provide further context to the role of each black coral VME. This area is influenced by very strong bottom currents. The resulting connectivity network was highly directed and relatively sparse with only 10 of the 64 possible links being realized reflecting the Both those strong bottom currents and the very short larval duration of the black coral. The 3 largest VMEs— BC1, BC2, and BC3— occurred on Flemish Cap. And of these, BC1 had the highest connectance linking to BC2 and BC4, while BC1 and BC2 also connected with each other. All 4 of the largest VMEs showed self-loops indicating larval retention and therefore the potential for self-recruitment. And simulations indicated that removal of BC1 would have the strongest effect on the natural connectivity network, followed by removal of BC3. Areas such as BC1 and BC2 may warrant particular attention because of their connectivity properties and location relative to climate refugia. So to summarize, present-day conservation areas closed to bottom contact fishing may remain relevant in the near term, especially on Flemish Cap, but their effectiveness as climate refugia is likely to decline substantially by mid to late century under most scenarios. This challenges the effectiveness of the current configuration of closed areas in future and supports the need for monitoring and periodic reevaluation. For black corals in NAFO, areas such as BC1 and BC2 may warrant particular attention because they combine present ecological significance relative persistence of analogue conditions in the short to medium term, and an important role in larval exchange, while also being at least partially protected by bottom fishery closures. The full results of the climate impact assessments will be presented at the November 2026 meeting of the NAFO Scientific Council Working Group on Ecosystem Science and Assessment, or WGESA. I'd like to leave you with this key message. End-of-century conservation, which is relevant to long-lived sessile marine species such as many VME indicators, depends on protection of environmentally analogous and connected areas. Thank you very much for your time today. Thank you.
